title: Details of violent arrest heard at coroner’s inquest
article: In less than 10 minutes, Regina police officers went from chasing Calvin Roy McLean to trying to keep his heart pumping when the 43-yearold suddenly went into medical distress during his arrest.

Const. Tyler Boynton was one of five officers who assisted in arresting McLean two years ago. That arrest involved two bursts of pepper spray and several officers holding McLean belly-down on the ground, his hands bound behind him by two sets of handcuffs linked together and a restraint strap on his legs, a coroner's inquest heard.

Boynton said that while officers were reading McLean his rights, they realized he wasn't responding to questions. They lifted him to his knees and saw a four-to-five inch pool of blood on the ground, and blood around his mouth, Boynton testified.
He said McLean appeared to take one breath as they placed him on his side, but he had no pulse. Officers began cardio-pulmonary resuscitation until paramedics arrived.
McLean died the next day in hospital.

Boynton told the inquest the only words he ever heard from McLean that night on Oct. 8, 2008, were, "Come on guys, come on," as if, in his opinion, McLean was asking the officers just to let him leave.

Monday marked the opening day for a week-long inquest probing McLean's death. Presiding coroner Darin Chow told the six jurors their task is not to assess blame, but they can make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths.

McLean's widow Andrea said she's relieved to finally have the inquest underway in hopes of shedding light on what happened to her husband and why. "My husband was somewhat athletic ... It just doesn't make any sense that he would have went into cardiac arrest," she said in an interview.

Lawyer Bob Hrycan, who represents McLean's widow, grilled the officers in cross-examination about their knowledge of "prone restraint asphyxia," and the effects of pepper spray combined with restraining a prisoner in a prone position. Both indicated they receiving training in that risk. "Sometimes, it's unavoidable," replied Const. Cory Longhurst, who had used the pepper spray, replied.
One of the jurors asked Boynton how he could distinguish between a person prone on the ground resisting arrest as opposed to struggling for air. "I don't think it's possible," he said.

Police first became involved with McLean when they were dispatched at 11:26 p.m. for a report of a man armed with an axe. Longhurst testified that he later learned from Andrea why her husband was so agitated that night - their daughter, 5 at the time of her father's death, had been the victim of an assault and charges had been dropped that day against one of those charged.
"It made sense why someone would be quite upset," said Longhurst, who didn't have that information until after McLean's arrest.

Longhurst was on his way to the call when a dispatcher indicated the armed man had gotten into a minivan. Longhurst spotted the van, and pursued it with lights and siren. When the van abruptly stopped, McLean exited and was yelling "something" that couldn't be heard above the siren. As Longhurst reached to turn off the siren, McLean took off running, with Longhurst and Boynton, who had just arrived, in pursuit on foot.

At one point, McLean tripped, and the officers began to close the distance. In the 2200 block of Quebec Street, McLean finally stopped, stood with his arms slightly out from his sides and the palms of his hands forward. Both Longhurst and Boynton believed that stance was aggressive. "It was obvious to me he was getting ready for a physical fight," Longhurst testified.
Both officers said they were shouting at McLean to get on the ground. "He kept walking at us not saying anything at all," said Longhurst. The officers backed up.
Longhurst fired a one-to-two-second burst of his pepper spray without much effect. Longhurst fired a second burst, and McLean squeezed his eyes shut and hunched over.

Longhurst and Boynton pushed him to the ground, one at each shoulder, holding McLean in a prone position to handcuff him. However, McLean had pulled his balled-up hands under his chest - which they took as resistance. "There's four of us still trying to get this guy's hands out," said Longhurst. McLean finally responded to a yelled command from Longhurst and brought out his left hand to be cuffed. But then the wrestling resumed, Longhurst said, adding a fifth officer was now on scene.

That's also when McLean's wife arrived. Longhurst said he stepped away to address Andrea. According to Longhurst, when he looked back, McLean was in an upright position, seated on his own and handcuffed on the sidewalk. Boynton, who did not recall McLean sitting, said the officers had managed to get another set of cuffs around his right hand, then linked the two sets. Because McLean's legs were flailing about, a restraint strap was put on above the knees. His rights were read about a minute later, he said.

Leaving the other officers to deal with McLean, Longhurst followed Andrea to their nearby house, where she explained why her husband was so distraught. Shortly after leaving, Longhurst heard the call for paramedics - not realizing it was for McLean until another officer came to get him.
